section.title: Confirming Your Calling and Election
section.sectionRationale: Having greeted his readers, Peter lays the foundation for the whole letter: God has already given everything needed for life and godliness. On that gift he builds a call to grow, listing the virtues that flow from faith and urging believers to make their calling and election sure.
section.thesis: Because God's divine power has already granted us everything for life and godliness and made us partakers of the divine nature, we make every effort to add virtue upon virtue, and so confirm our calling and secure a lavish entrance into Christ's eternal kingdom.
section.frameNote: Three movements: God's complete provision, verses 3 to 4; the virtues to add to faith, verses 5 to 7; and the fruit that confirms our calling, verses 8 to 11.

verses.text: His {{theia_dynamis|divine power}} has given us everything we need for life and {{eusebeia|godliness}} through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and {{arete|excellence}}.

Through these He has given us His precious and magnificent promises, so that through them you may become {{theias_physeos|partakers of the divine nature}}, now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires.
For this very reason, {{spoude|make every effort}} to add to your faith {{arete|virtue}}; and to virtue, {{gnosis|knowledge}};
and to knowledge, {{enkrateia|self-control}}; and to self-control, {{hypomone|perseverance}}; and to perseverance, godliness;
and to godliness, {{philadelphia|brotherly kindness}}; and to brotherly kindness, {{agape|love}}.

units.label: The fruit that confirms our calling
units.note: make your calling and election sure

verses.text: For if you possess these qualities and continue to grow in them, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your {{epignosis|knowledge}} of our Lord Jesus Christ.
But whoever lacks these traits is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten that he has been cleansed from his past sins.
Therefore, brothers, strive to make your {{ekloge|calling and election}} sure. For if you practice these things you will never stumble,
and you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

theia_dynamis.gloss: Divine power, the power that belongs to God alone. Peter says this power has already granted us everything needed for life and godliness. The Christian life begins not with human resolve but with God's own power supplying all we need in Christ.

eusebeia.gloss: Godliness, true reverence for God expressed in a devout life. It is both the aim of God's provision, everything for life and godliness, and one of the virtues to be added. Godliness is reverence toward God that shapes the whole of daily conduct.

arete.gloss: Excellence, moral virtue, goodness in action. It describes God's own excellence by which He called us, verse 3, and the virtue we add to faith, verse 5. The believer's goodness is a reflection of the moral excellence of the God who called him.

theias_physeos.gloss: The divine nature. Believers become partakers of the divine nature, sharing in God's moral character and life, not becoming gods themselves. Through God's promises His people are remade in holiness, escaping the world's corruption and growing to be like Him.

spoude.gloss: Diligence, earnest effort, eagerness. Make every effort translates this word. Because God has supplied everything, the believer responds not with passivity but with wholehearted diligence, applying himself to grow in grace.

gnosis.gloss: Knowledge, understanding, discernment. Added to virtue, it is practical spiritual insight that knows how to live rightly. It is closely related to the fuller epignosis of Christ, but here it names one link in the growing chain of Christian character.

enkrateia.gloss: Self-control, mastery over one's desires and impulses. It is the fruit of the Spirit that governs appetite and passion. Against teachers who promised freedom while enslaved to lust, Peter lists self-control as essential Christian growth.

hypomone.gloss: Perseverance, patient endurance, steadfastness under trial. It is the capacity to remain faithful and unmoved when pressure comes. In a letter awaiting the Day of the Lord, endurance keeps the believer on course to the end.

philadelphia.gloss: Brotherly kindness, affection for fellow believers as family. It is the warm, practical love that treats other Christians as true brothers and sisters. Peter places it just before love, the crown of the whole list.

agape.gloss: Love, the self-giving love that seeks the good of others, supremely shown in God. It stands at the summit of Peter's chain, the goal toward which every other virtue climbs. All growth in godliness culminates in love.

epignosis.gloss: Full, deep, personal knowledge of a person. Here it is knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. Growth in the virtues keeps this knowledge fruitful and effective, while their absence leaves a person blind and forgetful of his cleansing.

ekloge.gloss: Calling and election, God's summons and His choice of a people for Himself. Peter urges believers to make these sure, not by earning them but by confirming them through a fruitful life, so that assurance grows and the entrance into the kingdom is rich.

basic.context: Peter's argument begins here. First he says God has already given us everything we need to live a godly life, through knowing Christ, and has made us sharers in His own nature through great promises. Then, because of that gift, he urges us to work hard at growing, adding one virtue to another until we reach love. A growing Christian is fruitful and sure of his salvation; a stagnant one is blind and forgetful. So Peter says: confirm your calling by a fruitful life, and you will be richly welcomed into Christ's kingdom.
basic.hermeneutics: The order matters: grace first, then effort. God supplies everything, and precisely for that reason we make every effort. This is not earning salvation but confirming it. When Peter says make your calling and election sure, he means grow so that your assurance is grounded, not that you secure God's choice by works. The chain of virtues describes healthy growth, not a ladder we climb to be accepted.
basic.originalLanguages: God's theia dynamis, divine power, supplies all for life and eusebeia, godliness. Through His promises we share the theias physeos, the divine nature. So with spoude, diligence, we add to faith arete, virtue, then gnosis, self-control, hypomone, endurance, godliness, philadelphia, brotherly kindness, and at the summit agape, love. This keeps our epignosis of Christ fruitful and confirms our klesis kai ekloge, calling and election.
basic.typology: Sharing in the divine nature fulfills what humanity was made for, to bear God's image, marred in the fall and restored in Christ. The lavish entrance into the eternal kingdom points to the final homecoming foreshadowed throughout Scripture, the true promised land toward which all God's promises run.
basic.christ: It is through the knowledge of Christ that God's power grants all things for life and godliness. The precious promises are His, the divine nature is shared through union with Him, and the eternal kingdom belongs to our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Christ is the source of the provision, the sharer of the nature, and the King of the kingdom we enter.
basic.god: God is astonishingly generous: His divine power has already given everything we need, and His promises are precious and magnificent. He calls and chooses a people by His own glory and excellence. He is the God who supplies first and then invites His people to grow, so that all their diligence rests on His prior grace.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 5 lists the fruit of the Spirit, echoing Peter's virtues. Second Corinthians 3:18 speaks of being transformed into Christ's image, like partaking of the divine nature. Ephesians 2:8-10 holds grace and good works together. And Philippians 2:12-13 says to work out salvation because God works in us.
basic.oneStory: Humanity was made to share God's life and lost it through sin. In Christ, God restores that calling, granting by His power all that is needed for life and godliness and remaking His people in His own nature. The growing life of virtue that Peter describes is the renewed image of God taking shape, headed for the eternal kingdom that crowns the whole biblical story.

context.literary:
The passage is a single long argument built in three steps, and the hinge is the phrase 'for this very reason' at the start of verse 5. Everything before it, verses 3 and 4, is a sentence about what God has done, and everything after it is a sentence about what the readers are to do. The order is the point. Peter does not start with a demand and then supply the power; he starts with the power and lets it generate the demand. A reader who reverses the order and treats verses 5 to 7 as a ladder to climb has read the passage upside down.

Verses 3 and 4 are carried by a string of participles and relative clauses, so that God's gift is described in layers: His power has granted everything, through the knowledge of the one who called us, by His own glory and excellence, through which He has granted the promises, so that we might share in the divine nature. Verses 5 to 7 then shift to a rhetorical device the Greeks called a chain or climax, in which each link takes up the last: faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness, love. Paul uses the same device in Romans 5:3-5 and 8:29-30. The chain begins in faith, the root, and ends in love, the summit, and each of the middle terms is a different aspect of the one life.

Verses 8 to 11 give the consequence in two parallel pictures, one positive and one negative. If these qualities are present and growing, they keep you from being idle and fruitless; if they are lacking, the person is blind and has forgotten his cleansing. The command of verse 10, 'strive to make your calling and election sure,' sits at the centre, and verse 11 gives the reward, an entrance richly supplied into the eternal kingdom.

The passage also does something the letter does as a whole. It plants the word 'knowledge' at both ends, verse 3 and verse 8, so that the whole chain is enclosed by the knowing of Christ, and it begins the long defence against teachers who claim a knowledge without the life.
context.historical:
Peter's readers lived in a world whose moral philosophy had its own long lists of virtues. Greek writers spoke of a moral excellence they called arete, and a word that meant piety toward the gods, eusebeia, was a common name for the dutiful life. Self-control, enkrateia, was one of the highest ideals. When the Christian letters speak of these things they are speaking a language their readers knew. Peter takes these words and gives them a new source and a new end, by tying them to God's gift and to Jesus Christ.

The idea of sharing in the divine nature also had a pagan background. Greek and Roman thought spoke of the gods as immortal and of humans as mortal, and some thinkers spoke of the soul as escaping into the divine realm. The false teachers Peter has in mind may have used such language to promise a spiritual elevation apart from moral change. Peter uses the phrase but grounds it in the promises of God and, at once, in an escape from the corruption caused by desire. He turns a vocabulary of escape from the body into a vocabulary of moral transformation.

The false teachers, chapter 2 shows, were driven by greed and sensual desire. They promised freedom and were slaves of corruption, 2:19. They denied the Master and mocked the promise of His coming, 3:4. Peter's list of virtues is therefore a direct answer. The knowledge that matters is the knowledge of Christ, and it produces self-control, perseverance and love. Where those are missing, whatever the teacher claims, the knowledge is false.

The language of an 'entrance' in verse 11 would have been understood in two ways. In the ancient world a victor in the games or a king returning in triumph was received with a lavish welcome, and the verb for what is supplied was one used for the sponsor who paid for a city's choir. For a reader who knew the Old Testament the word recalled Israel's entrance into the land of promise. Peter uses both pictures, a welcome and a homecoming.
context.canonical:
Peter's chain of virtues belongs among the New Testament's lists of Christian character. Paul names the fruit of the Spirit, 'love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control,' Galatians 5:22-23, and tells the Colossians to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, and over all of it 'put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity,' Colossians 3:12-14. In each of these lists love governs the rest, as it does here, and the Christian life is described as fruit and clothing, not a ladder.

The idea that God supplies the power to live this life runs through Paul as well. 'It is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose,' Philippians 2:13, is the ground of 'work out your salvation,' 2:12, just as Peter's verse 3 is the ground of his verse 5. Ephesians 2:8-10 joins the two in a single passage: we are saved by grace through faith, and we are 'God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works.'

The theme of restored likeness to God appears at the start of the Bible, Genesis 1:26-27, where humans are made in God's image, and is picked up when Paul says believers have 'put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator,' Colossians 3:10, and are being 'transformed into His image with intensifying glory,' 2 Corinthians 3:18. John says that when Christ appears we will be like Him, 1 John 3:2. Peter's 'partakers of the divine nature' belongs with these.

The command to make the calling sure has a sister in Hebrews 6:11, 'show this same diligence to the very end, in order to make your hope sure.' And the picture of a barren branch against a fruitful one is Jesus' own, John 15:1-8, where He prunes the fruitful and removes the fruitless, and tells His followers that apart from Him they can do nothing.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter wants his readers to be grounded before they are warned. The people who are about to be attacked by false teaching need to know that they already possess everything, and the opening sentence is built to say so: it has been given, it is complete, it covers life and godliness. This is not a motivational opening to be left behind. It is the foundation for the rest of the letter, since the false teachers will promise something more and Peter has told the readers in advance that there is nothing more to be had.

The list of virtues is meant as growth that cannot be separated from faith. He wants the readers to see that a faith which stays alone is not what the gospel produces. He is not describing the rungs of a ladder but the natural fruit of a life that has been joined to Christ. The call to 'make every effort' is therefore a call to cooperate with what God is already doing, and the whole chain is bracketed by the promises and the kingdom, so that a reader never loses sight of where the effort comes from and where it leads.

The warning of verse 9 is meant to sting a little. The person who lacks these qualities has forgotten that he has been cleansed, and Peter wants the readers to remember. The remedy for a barren life is not more rules but a remembered cleansing. And the promise of verse 11 is meant to draw them forward. A lavish welcome awaits those who finish well, and Peter wants them to run toward it, not out of fear but out of confident expectation.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 3 and 4 describe what God has done, and the right response to them is gratitude and trust, not effort. Verses 5 to 7 are prescription: add these qualities, with every effort. Verse 10 is a command, to strive, and verse 8 and verse 11 are conditional descriptions of what follows. The passage must be read in that order, or it will be turned into a recipe for earning what has already been given.

The list of eight qualities is not a fixed syllabus. Other New Testament lists have different items and different orders, and Peter chose these for his readers' situation, where false teaching had loosened both knowledge and conduct. It would be a mistake to turn the list into a checklist, or to think that one must master the first before moving to the second. The point is that all of them belong to a life in Christ, and that they grow together.

The statement that those who lack these things are blind and forgetful is a description of the state of such a person, not a prescription for how to treat them. It does not give believers the right to pronounce on one another's standing. It is a warning addressed to the readers about themselves.

Finally, the promise of a lavish entrance is an encouragement and not a transaction. Verse 11 does not say that effort buys the kingdom, but that those who have been growing will find the way richly opened. Peter's logic is not 'work to be accepted' but 'since you have been given everything, live as people who have.'

debates.question: What does it mean to be 'partakers of the divine nature'?

views.label: A renewal of character through union with Christ
views.case: The sentence runs straight on to 'now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires,' and the whole of verses 5 to 7 is about moral growth. The passage speaks of a new character, a likeness to God in holiness, in line with Ephesians 4:24, 'created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.' This is the usual Protestant reading.

views.label: Participation in God's life, as in the Eastern tradition
views.case: Eastern writers such as Athanasius took the verse as the basis for saying that God became man so that man might share in the life of God. They hold that creatures remain creatures and that the participation is in God's gifts and energies, not in His essence. They see 2 Peter 1:4 together with John 17:21-23 and 2 Corinthians 3:18.

views.label: A claim to become divine in nature
views.case: Some pagan readers and later mystics took such words to mean absorption into the divine. Peter's context excludes this, since the word 'promises' keeps the gift outside us and ahead of us, and the next verse is about growing virtues. The Creator and creature distinction runs throughout Scripture.

debates.bearing: The first two readings agree on the essential point: the passage speaks of real transformation by grace, never of becoming God. The verse is also a promise, 'through them you may become,' so the full sharing awaits the day we see Him and are like Him, 1 John 3:2.

debates.question: Does 'make your calling and election sure' mean we secure our own salvation?

views.label: We confirm what God has done by growing in fruitfulness
views.case: God does the calling and choosing, and the passage began with His power and promises. The Greek word for 'sure' is a legal term for a guarantee. Believers strengthen their own certainty and show others that the call is real by the life they live. Philippians 2:12-13 holds the same balance.

views.label: Perseverance is the necessary path of the elect
views.case: The warning is real, and the passage says the person who lacks these qualities has forgotten his cleansing. The reformers taught that those whom God elects persevere, and that the lasting fruit of perseverance is the means by which election is made visible, in line with John 15:1-8 and Hebrews 6:11-12.

views.label: A warning that a person can fall away
views.case: Some understand 'never stumble' and the lavish entrance as conditional, so that a believer who fails to grow may forfeit the entrance. They point to the warnings in Hebrews and to the command to 'strive.' Other readers answer that Peter's word 'stumble' is not the same as 'fall' and that the verb is used of all believers, James 3:2.

debates.bearing: All three readings take the warning seriously, and all see the effort as a response to God's gift. What the text does not say is that we can earn election. The point of the diligence is to live in the light of what God has already done, and to find in a growing life the evidence that the call is real.

debates.question: Is the chain of virtues a sequence of stages?

views.label: A progression, each quality built on the last
views.case: The Greek wording says 'in your faith supply virtue, in virtue knowledge,' and so on. Each is a prerequisite for the next. A person must have moral resolve before understanding, understanding before discipline, and so forth, ending in love.

views.label: A set of interlocking qualities that grow together
views.case: The same chain-style appears in Romans 5:3-5, where the links are not strictly sequential, and other lists in the New Testament have the same items in a different order. Peter's point is that no quality stands alone, not that one must be finished before the next begins.

debates.bearing: The chain does teach that each quality needs the others and that love is the crown. It should not be read as a rule that a believer must reach one level before the next, since all grow from the same faith.

study.originalLanguages:
Peter begins with 'divine power,' theia dynamis, an adjective that was common in Greek religious speech and rare in the Bible, and the verb 'has given,' dedoremenes, is a perfect participle from a word for a gift, doreomai, as when Pilate granted Jesus' body in Mark 15:45. The perfect tense speaks of a gift given once with lasting result, and the word itself is the opposite of earning. 'Godliness' is eusebeia, reverence toward God shown in conduct; it appears three times in this chapter, 1:3, 1:6 and 1:7, and again in 3:11. 'Excellence' is arete, which occurs only four times in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:8, 1 Peter 2:9, and twice here, 1:3 and 1:5. In 1 Peter 2:9 it is God's excellences that the people proclaim, and in 2 Peter 1:3 it is God's own excellence that calls us. In verse 5 the same word names the quality we are to add, so the human virtue is a reflection of the divine.

Verse 4 gives the phrase 'partakers of the divine nature,' theias physeos koinonoi. The word koinonos, a partner or sharer, is the same word Peter used of himself in 1 Peter 5:1, 'a partaker of the glory to be revealed.' The noun physis, nature, is used in the New Testament of what a thing is by origin, as in Galatians 4:8 where the Galatians had served those who 'by nature are not gods,' and Ephesians 2:3. The 'corruption,' phthora, is decay and ruin, as in 2:12 and 2:19 and Romans 8:21, and it is joined to epithymia, the desires that drive it.

In verse 5 the verb 'add,' epichoregeo, is richer than the English. The root belongs to the choregos, the wealthy citizen who paid for the chorus in a city's drama and did so lavishly, and the verb means to supply fully. Paul uses it of God who 'supplies' seed, 2 Corinthians 9:10, and the Spirit, Galatians 3:5. Peter's readers are to supply their faith with virtue as a sponsor supplies a chorus. The verb returns at the other end in verse 11, where the entrance 'will be richly provided,' using the same verb. They supply virtue; God supplies the entrance. 'Make every effort' is spoude, eagerness or haste, a word of earnest diligence that Hebrews 6:11 shares.

The terms of the chain each carry a particular colour. Gnosis is knowledge applied, practical insight. Enkrateia, 'self-control,' is mastery over appetite and is named among the fruit of the Spirit, Galatians 5:23. Hypomone, 'perseverance,' literally remaining under a load, is the steadiness in trial that Romans 5:3-4 and James 1:3-4 praise. Philadelphia is the love of brothers, Romans 12:10, and agape is the self-giving love that Christ commanded, John 13:34-35. Classical lists of virtues seldom if ever gave a place to agape, and putting it at the summit is one of Peter's most distinctive moves.

In verse 8 the readers are saved from being 'ineffective and unproductive,' argos and akarpos, idle and fruitless. In verse 9 the unusual word myopazon, 'nearsighted,' appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and it gives us the English word myopic. The person who lacks these qualities sees only what is close at hand. 'Cleansed' is katharismos, a cleansing, the same word that Hebrews 1:3 uses of Christ's making purification for sins.

The verse 10 phrase 'make your calling and election sure' uses bebaian poieisthai, to make firm. Bebaios is a legal and commercial word for a guarantee that holds, and Hebrews 6:19 calls hope an anchor that is 'sure and steadfast.' Klesis, calling, and ekloge, election, are paired here as two sides of one reality, God's summons and God's choice. And 'you will never stumble' is the strong negative ou me ptaisete pote; the verb ptaio means to trip, and Romans 11:11 distinguishes stumbling from falling, while James 3:2 says all stumble in many ways, so Peter must mean a final failure and not a trip. Finally, 'entrance' in verse 11 is eisodos, as in Hebrews 10:19, where believers have confidence to enter the sanctuary.

typology.type: Humanity made in God's image, restored in Christ
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 1:26-27 says God made man in His image and likeness, the first statement of what humanity is for. Sin marred it, and the Bible describes its restoration in Christ, who is 'the image of the invisible God,' Colossians 1:15, and in whom believers 'put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator,' Colossians 3:10. Peter's 'partakers of the divine nature' is the same hope in other words, and it comes with a promise, as John says, that 'when Christ appears, we will be like Him,' 1 John 3:2. The correspondence is real but incomplete in this life, since the likeness is still growing and will not be finished until the end.

typology.type: The exodus from corruption and the entrance into the land
typology.fulfillment: Israel was brought out of Egypt and into a good land 'where you will lack nothing,' Deuteronomy 8:7-9. Peter speaks of believers who have 'escaped the corruption in the world' and who will receive a richly supplied entrance into the eternal kingdom, 1:4 and 1:11, and he will call his own death an exodus, 1:15. Hebrews says that 'the promise of entering His rest still stands,' Hebrews 4:1, so the land was a picture. The escalation is from a strip of earth to an eternal kingdom of the Lord and Savior. The type falls short because Israel's entrance could be lost by unbelief, and the writers of the New Testament use this warning to urge diligence.

typology.type: The fruitful vine and the barren branch
typology.fulfillment: Israel was God's vineyard, planted on a fertile hill, but the fruit it produced was sour, Isaiah 5:1-2. Jesus says that He is the true vine and the Father is the keeper of the vineyard, that He removes the fruitless branch and prunes the fruitful one, and that apart from Him His followers can do nothing, John 15:1-8. Peter's picture of the believer who is 'ineffective and unproductive' or fruitful in the knowledge of the Lord belongs to the same family. Where Israel failed to bear fruit, the branch in Christ does, and the fruit comes from the vine, not from the branch's own resources. The picture does not settle the debates about perseverance, but it makes the dependence plain.

typology.type: The righteous tree beside the streams
typology.fulfillment: Psalm 1:3 describes the one who delights in the law as 'like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season.' Peter's growing believer, steady in virtue and fruitful in knowledge, is the New Testament form of the same man. The escalation is that the stream is now the knowledge of Christ and the fruit is love, Galatians 5:22. The correspondence is of theme and not of a single event, and Peter does not cite the psalm, so it should be taken as a likeness and not as a fulfilment.

study.christ:
Christ is named at the end of each of the passage's three sections, and each time he is named differently. In verses 3 and 4 He is the one who called us, and the one in whom we know God. In verse 8 He is 'our Lord Jesus Christ,' the object of the knowledge that keeps us fruitful. In verse 11 He is 'our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ,' the king of the eternal kingdom. The passage begins in His call, grows in His knowledge and ends in His kingdom.

The gift of verse 3 is given 'through the knowledge of Him who called us.' The Greek can refer to the Father or to Christ, and the word 'called' is regularly used of the Father in Peter's letters, 1 Peter 1:15, 2:9 and 5:10. But in verse 2 the knowledge was 'of God and of Jesus our Lord,' and the next verse speaks of one source, so the knowledge of the caller and the knowledge of the Lord are not separate acts. To know Jesus is to know the one who calls, and the gift of everything for life and godliness is received there.

The 'promises' of verse 4 are His. Paul says that all of God's promises find their 'Yes' in Christ, 2 Corinthians 1:20, and the promises Peter has in mind, a share in God's nature and an entrance into the eternal kingdom, are given to those who are united to Him. In Romans 8:29 the purpose of God is that His people be 'conformed to the image of His Son,' which is the clearest statement of what Peter means by sharing the divine nature. Christ is the pattern of the new humanity. He is the one in whom the likeness of God is fully seen, Colossians 1:15, and believers are made to resemble Him.

The cleansing of verse 9 is His work. To forget that one has been cleansed from past sins is to forget the cross, and Peter has already said in his first letter that Christ 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. The remedy for the blind and forgetful person is to look back at what Christ did.

Finally, the kingdom is His. 'The eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ' joins two titles of authority, and it is the kingdom Daniel saw given to the Son of Man and the saints, Daniel 7:27, an 'everlasting kingdom.' Believers enter it not as visitors but as members of the king's own household. The lavish reception of verse 11 is the welcome that He gives.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Peter's virtues are not codes for Jesus' qualities, and the chain is not an allegory. The link to Christ is that He is the source, the knowledge, the cleanser and the king.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the one who gives first. 'His divine power has given us everything we need,' and the verb is in the perfect tense of a completed gift. Peter does not describe a God who offers help for those who have done their best; he describes one who has already supplied all that life and godliness require. Whatever the readers will go on to do in verses 5 to 7, they are doing it out of a store they already hold.

He is a God who calls by His own glory and excellence. The call is not a general invitation but a summons that draws on His own character. Peter's word for excellence, arete, is the same word used in 1 Peter 2:9 for the praiseworthy acts of God that His people are to proclaim, so the God who calls is the God whose goodness is the reason to call. The calling does not depend on the response, since it springs from what God is.

He is a God of promises. Verse 4 calls them 'precious and magnificent,' and they are the means through which a new nature is given. God's word is the instrument of His work, and His promises are not decoration. A God who speaks a promise has already begun to keep it. This is why the Bible's stress on promise, from the call of Abraham onward, is not a delay but a down payment.

He is a God who transforms. The aim of the gift is that we share His nature, escaping the corruption that desire brings. The God of the Bible is not content to forgive and leave people as they were. He is holy, and He makes His people share in His holiness, Hebrews 12:10. Paul says the same: 'He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion,' Philippians 1:6.

He is a God who works through human effort without being replaced by it. Peter holds the two together in one breath: 'His divine power has given' and 'make every effort.' Paul does so too, Philippians 2:12-13. God's sovereignty does not make human diligence unnecessary, and human diligence does not become a rival to His grace. The God who supplies is the God who commands, and He is the one who supplies the entrance at the end, 1:11.

He is a God of a kingdom that lasts. The 'eternal kingdom' echoes the Old Testament's assurance that His kingdom is everlasting and His dominion endures through all generations, Psalm 145:13. The God of Peter's letter is not threatened by false teachers or by the passing of the age, and He will bring His people home.

For worship, the passage teaches thanks before effort. The proper first response to verses 3 and 4 is to stop and see how much has been given, and then to go and live as people who are rich.

crossReferences.note: Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, and adds that against such things there is no law. Peter's list overlaps in self-control, perseverance and love, and, like Paul's, treats the qualities as fruit that grows from a life in union with God and not as achievements.

Paul tells the believers to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, because it is God who works in them to will and to act. This is the same logic as 2 Peter 1:3-5, where God's gift of everything is the reason for every effort. Effort and grace are not rivals.

We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and yet we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand. The passage holds together what Peter holds together, a salvation that is wholly a gift and a life of effort that follows from it.

Believers with unveiled faces reflect the glory of the Lord and are being transformed into His image with ever increasing glory. This is the process Peter has in mind when he speaks of sharing in the divine nature, a progressive change that comes from the Lord through the Spirit and not from the believer's own power.

Paul traces a chain of its own, from suffering to perseverance, from perseverance to character, and from character to hope, and says that hope does not disappoint because God has poured out His love into our hearts. It shows that the New Testament writers used a stepwise sequence to describe growth, and that love poured out by God is the ground.

The new self is 'being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator.' Knowledge and the image of God are joined here as in Peter's passage, where knowledge of Christ is the way into a divine likeness. The renewal is a process that goes on in the present.

Jesus is the true vine; the Father removes the fruitless branch and prunes the fruitful one, and apart from Him His followers can do nothing. The language of fruit and barrenness in 2 Peter 1:8 belongs to the same picture, and the dependence on Christ stands behind the whole of Peter's call to grow.

The writer wants his readers to show the same diligence to the very end 'in order to make your hope sure,' so that they will not be sluggish but will imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and patience. The wording is very close to Peter's command to make the calling sure, and it joins diligence, hope and the promises.

Paul sets out God's purpose from foreknowledge to glory, so that His people are conformed to the image of His Son. It is the same chain of calling and election that Peter has in mind, and it shows why he can say that those whom God calls will enter the kingdom: the work is God's from beginning to end.

Now we are children of God, and when Christ appears we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is. John looks to the end of the process that Peter calls sharing in the divine nature, and he gives the reason why it is promised, that the final sight of Christ completes the likeness.

The letter ends with the command to grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. The terms are those of the opening, grace and knowledge, and the instruction sums up the lesson of chapter 1 for the whole letter, that growth is the shape of the Christian life.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a creature made in the likeness of God and set in a world where God was near, Genesis 1:26-27. The fall broke that likeness. Humanity became subject to corruption and death, Romans 8:21, and the story of Scripture is the story of how God restores what was lost. Peter's phrase 'partakers of the divine nature' is a short summary of where that story is heading.

The restoring begins with a call. God called Abraham out of a world of idols, brought Israel out of Egypt, and gave them promises, and Peter says the promises are now fulfilled in Christ, who has given us 'precious and magnificent promises.' The exodus pattern lies behind the passage, with an escape from corruption and an entrance into a kingdom. In his own death, Peter says in 1:15, he will make his own exodus, and the word he chooses is the one used of Moses and Elijah talking with Jesus about His departure on the mountain, Luke 9:31.

The middle of the story is a time of growth. The people of God are called to bear fruit, as Israel was meant to be a fruitful vine, Isaiah 5:1-2, and as Jesus says His followers are, John 15:1-8. The virtues Peter lists are the shape that the restored image takes while the believer is still on the way, as Paul says, 'being transformed into His image with intensifying glory,' 2 Corinthians 3:18. The life is not an achievement. It is the fruit of what God supplied in the beginning, and it is lived in the company of other believers, in love, which is the crown of the chain.

The story is also one of warning. Israel failed to enter the land through unbelief, Hebrews 3 and 4, and Peter's readers are called to diligence so that they will not fall short. The warning is part of the way God brings His people home.

The end of the story is the one Peter names in verse 11, an entrance into the eternal kingdom of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. In Revelation the kingdom is the new heaven and earth where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3, and 2 Peter 3:13 describes it as the place where righteousness is at home. The corruption has gone, the likeness is complete, and those who have been made partakers of the divine nature see Him as He is, 1 John 3:2. The call that began the story ends in a welcome.

sermon.title: The Great Escape
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in 2 Peter, this message on 2 Peter 1:8-11 handles the fruit of the virtues, the danger of barrenness, and the call to make your calling and election sure, the climax of this movement. A clear, orthodox treatment of assurance grounded in a fruitful life.

quiz.q: What is the foundation on which Peter builds his call to grow?

options.text: God's divine power has already given us everything we need for life and godliness.
options.note: Verse 3: grace and provision come first, then the call to effort.

options.text: Our own determination to become better people.
options.note: Effort matters, but it rests on God's prior provision, not on self-will.

options.text: The precious promises God has given, which we must complete ourselves.
options.note: The promises are central, but Peter stresses God has already given all we need.

options.text: The idea that God helps those who first help themselves.
options.note: The passage reverses this: God gives everything first, then we respond.

quiz.q: What does it mean to become partakers of the divine nature?

options.text: To be transformed into God's moral likeness through union with Christ, escaping the world's corruption.
options.note: Verse 4 keeps the meaning ethical and relational, real transformation, not becoming gods.

options.text: To share in God's life and character by grace while remaining creatures.
options.note: True, but it should be stated clearly that we never cross into being God in essence.

options.text: To literally become gods ourselves.
options.note: The Creator-creature distinction always stands; this is transformation, not deification into deity.

options.text: To gain secret spiritual powers over others.
options.note: The context is holiness and escaping corruption, not power over others.

quiz.q: Where does Peter's chain of virtues finally lead?

options.text: To love, the crown of the whole list.
options.note: Verse 7: every virtue climbs toward agape, love.

options.text: To knowledge, the highest Christian attainment.
options.note: Knowledge is one link, not the summit; love is the goal.

options.text: To brotherly kindness among believers.
options.note: Brotherly kindness comes just before the true summit, love.

options.text: To self-control as the ultimate mark of maturity.
options.note: Self-control is early in the chain, not its climax.

quiz.q: What does Peter mean by make your calling and election sure?

options.text: Confirm God's gracious choice by a fruitful, growing life, so that your assurance is grounded.
options.note: Verse 10: effort confirms what God has done; it does not earn it.

options.text: Persevere in fruitfulness, the path by which the elect reach the kingdom.
options.note: True and complementary, though the emphasis is on confirming, not securing, election.

options.text: Earn your salvation by accumulating enough good works.
options.note: Salvation is God's gift; the fruit confirms it rather than buying it.

options.text: Simply feel more confident without any change in life.
options.note: Assurance here is grounded in real, visible growth, not mere feeling.

quiz.q: What is true of the believer who lacks these growing qualities?

options.text: He is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten he was cleansed from his sins.
options.note: Verse 9 diagnoses spiritual blindness and forgetfulness of grace.

options.text: He is simply a slower grower who need not be concerned.
options.note: Peter treats barrenness as a serious warning, not a mild condition.

options.text: He is fruitful in Christ regardless of his conduct.
options.note: The opposite: without the virtues he is ineffective and unfruitful.

options.text: He has lost sight of the grace that first cleansed him.
options.note: True to verse 9, though it understates the strong image of blindness.

questions: Peter says God has already given everything you need for life and godliness. Where are you living as though you lacked what God has in fact supplied?
The virtues build one upon another toward love. Which link in the chain, self-control, perseverance, brotherly kindness, is God calling you to grow in right now?
A barren believer forgets he was cleansed from his sins. How does remembering your own forgiveness fuel your desire to grow?
Peter urges us to confirm our calling by a fruitful life. What is one habit you could begin this week that would make your assurance more grounded?
The goal is a lavish welcome into Christ's eternal kingdom. How does keeping that homecoming in view change the way you spend today?

translationNotes.note: Called us by His own glory and excellence renders a phrase a footnote allows to read to His own glory and excellence; either way God's own character is the source of the call.
Partakers of the divine nature translates theias physeos; it means sharing God's moral character and life through Christ, not becoming God in essence.
The chain of virtues uses a rhetorical device where each grace supplies the next, from faith through self-control and endurance up to love.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 2 Peter 1:3-11.
